claims.source: In particular, we found fibrous patterns of higher elastic modulus congregating at sites of indenting regions (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by AFM stiffness mapping data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Staining for cellulose in mesophyll cells of wheat that exhibit alternating patterns of lobe-like outgrowth and indenting regions shows a strong presence of cellulose in the constricted regions of the cells.
claims.source: Staining for cellulose in mesophyll cells of wheat that exhibit alternating patterns of lobe like outgrowth and indenting regions has shown a strong presence of cellulose in the constricted regions of the cells (Jung and Wernicke, 1990).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jung and Wernicke, 1990.

claims.claim: Cellulose microfibrils act as a brace around the indenting regions providing mechanical reinforcement of those regions.
claims.source: Altogether, this suggests that CMFs act as a brace around the indenting regions providing mechanical reinforcement of those regions.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined evidence of AFM stiffness maps, cellulose staining, and microtubule organization patterns.

claims.claim: Inner microtubule arrays in pavement cells appear to be identical to those observed on the outer face.
claims.source: The inner MT arrays appear to be identical to those observed on the outer face, thereby suggesting the cell walls of the indenting regions are reinforced on both faces of the cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy imaging of microtubules on both inner and outer faces of pavement cells.

claims.claim: Pavement cell shape is maintained by localized microtubule-dependent wall reinforcements in indenting regions.
claims.source: These data thus consolidate a model in which pavement cell shape is maintained by localized MT-dependent wall reinforcements in indenting regions (Fu et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the combined data from AFM, microtubule imaging, and is consistent with a previously published model.

claims.claim: Physical models of the shoot apical meristem as a pressurized vessel show that supracellular mechanical stress pattern can prescribe global microtubule organization and tissue morphology.
claims.source: Physical models of the shoot apical meristem as a pressurized vessel have shown that the supracellular mechanical stress pattern can prescribe global MT organization and tissue morphology (Hamant et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hamant et al., 2008.

claims.claim: The 3D finite element model shows a strong anisotropic arrangement of stresses focused in indenting regions of pavement cells.
claims.source: The outcome of the model with mechanically isotropic cell walls showed a strong anisotropic arrangement of stresses focused in indenting regions of the pavement cells (Figure 2A,C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 2A,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: There is a good correlation between the largest stress direction and microtubule arrangement in pavement cells.
claims.source: Despite the noisy behavior of MTs in pavement cells, visualization of MT organization with YFP:MBD (Wightman and Turner, 2007) showed a good correlation between the largest stress direction and MT arrangement, aggregating in indenting regions of the pavement cells (Figure 2B,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of computational model predictions with experimental microtubule imaging data.

claims.claim: The clustering of microtubule arrays in the indenting regions correlates with regions of predicted higher magnitude of stress.
claims.source: Furthermore, the clustering of MT arrays in the indenting regions also correlated with regions of predicted higher magnitude of stress (Figure 1E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of computational model predictions with experimental microtubule imaging data.

claims.claim: A 3D pavement cell model including anticlinal and bottom walls generates principal stress tensor direction patterns similar to the curved surface model.
claims.source: Stress directions were also computed in a model representing a 3D pavement cell shape along with the anticlinal and bottom walls. The model generated principal stress tensor direction pattern similar to the curved surface model (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results comparing different model geometries.

claims.claim: Higher magnitude of tensile stresses are observed in the indenting neck-like regions, matching the local microtubule pattern.
claims.source: Both cases showed a higher magnitude of tensile stresses in the indenting neck-like regions, matching the local MT pattern; compression forces at approximately 10% of the tension value were observed in some regions close to the cell boundary with no clear relation with MT behavior (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D–F.

claims.claim: Tensile stress influences microtubule organization at a subcellular level in pavement cells.
claims.source: This suggests that tensile stress influences MT organization at a subcellular level in pavement cells, thereby indicating that the perception of stress must involve a mechanism that acts locally within each cell, rather than on a cell-wide or tissue-wide basis.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between predicted stress patterns and observed microtubule organization at subcellular resolution.

claims.claim: For small elastic deformations, the overall stress pattern is affected more strongly by the geometry of the cells than by the mechanical anisotropy of the existing cell wall material.
claims.source: The simulations thus suggest that for small elastic deformations the overall stress pattern is affected more strongly by the geometry of the cells than by the mechanical anisotropy of the existing cell wall material.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results comparing isotropic and anisotropic material properties.

claims.claim: Assuming the epidermis is under tension, the largest stress direction should be circumferential around a local bump.
claims.source: In particular, assuming that the epidermis is under tension, the largest stress direction should be circumferential around a local bump.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on computational modeling predictions under specific assumptions about tissue mechanics.

claims.claim: Microtubule arrays around elevated guard cells show circumferential orientations, consistent with predicted stress directions.
claims.source: Stomata being often in such an elevated position, we analyzed the MT arrays around guard cells and we found circumferential orientations, consistent with the predicted stress directions (Figure 2F,G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of computational model predictions with experimental microtubule imaging data around stomata.

claims.claim: No circumferential microtubule pattern is observed near stomata that are not elevated.
claims.source: Conversely, no circumferential MT pattern could be observed near stomata that were not elevated (Figures 2H,I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental microtubule imaging data comparing elevated and non-elevated stomata.

claims.claim: Patterns of cellular and supracellular mechanical stress and microtubule orientation are correlated.
claims.source: The results suggest that, analogously to what was observed in the shoot meristem, patterns of cellular and supracellular mechanical stress and MT orientation are correlated.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined evidence of computational modeling and experimental observations, and is consistent with previous findings in shoot meristem.

claims.claim: The correlation between mechanical stress patterns and microtubule orientation holds down to the sub-cellular level.
claims.source: Furthermore, we find that this correlation holds down to the sub-cellular level.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of stress-microtubule correlations at subcellular resolution in pavement cells.

claims.claim: Application of compressive forces results in an increase in overall stress in physical models.
claims.source: Our finite element model predicts that when subjected to compression from above, there is an increase in overall stress in physical models (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: Compression of cotyledon pavement cells results in flattening of cells.
claims.source: Depth color-coded Z stacks of MT organization and transects of the confocal Z-stack showed flattening of cells due to compression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy imaging data showing cell morphology changes under compression.

claims.claim: Microtubule anisotropy increases significantly 7 hours after compression, with mean ± SE of 0.37 ± 0.06 at 0 hr (n = 95 cells, 5 seedlings) and 0.57 ± 0.06 at 7 hr (n = 95 cells; 5 seedlings; p<0.0001; Mann–Whitney U test).
claims.source: Imaging of MTs in the cells immediately after and 7 hr after compression showed rearrangement of MTs into more aligned arrays by 7 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D,F; Video 1; mean ± SE is 0.37 ± 0.06 for 0 hr, n = 95 cells, 5 seedlings and 0.57 ± 0.06 for 7 hr, n = 95 cells; 5 seedlings; p<0.0001; Mann–Whitney U test; Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of microtubule anisotropy with statistical significance testing.

claims.claim: Increased microtubule anisotropy persists for longer periods when the tissue is maintained in the compressed condition.
claims.source: This increased MT anisotropy persisted for longer periods when the tissue was maintained in the compressed condition (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The microtubule response to compression is reversible: 24 hours following removal of compression, nematic tensor values for microtubule anisotropy are reduced to a value close to that obtained during the time point immediately after compression (mean ± SE is 0.24 ± 0.02).
claims.source: This response was also reversible: 24 hr following removal of compression, nematic tensor values for MT anisotropy were reduced to a value close to that obtained during the time point immediately after compression (mean ± SE is 0.24 ± 0.02; Figure 3E,G,H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of microtubule anisotropy before, during, and after compression.

claims.claim: Large cuts in cotyledons result in immediate outward displacement of the cut edges, consistent with release of tension.
claims.source: Macroscopically, large cuts in cotyledons resulted in an immediate outward displacement of the cut edges, consistent with release of tension (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B; Video 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data showing tissue deformation after cutting.

claims.claim: Upward movement of mesophyll cells is observed after large cuts, consistent with the epidermis being under tension.
claims.source: We also observed upward movement of mesophyll cells from the layer below (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C), consistent with the epidermis being under tension as observed in other plant tissues (Kutschera and Niklas, 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and is consistent with previously published findings in other plant tissues.

claims.claim: The physical model predicts that maximal stress directions become circumferential to the laceration after treatment and independent of cell geometry.
claims.source: Our physical model suggests that maximal stress directions become circumferential to the laceration after treatment and independent of cell geometry (Figure 3A,B; Video 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 3A,B and Video 3.

claims.claim: After large-scale laceration, hyper-aligned microtubule arrays are observed in cells adjacent to the damaged region at 3.5 hours, and the alignment advances to cell layers farther away from the site of laceration at 7 hours, independently of cell shape.
claims.source: Time series imaging of MT rearrangements showed a progressive change in the organization of MT arrays around the site. After 3.5 hr, we observed hyper-aligned MT arrays in cells adjacent to the damaged region and at 7 hr the alignment advanced to cell layers farther away from the site of laceration, independently of cell shape (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data showing progressive microtubule reorganization after laceration.

claims.claim: Microtubule anisotropy increases significantly 7 hours after laceration, with mean ± SE of 0.080 ± 0.007 at 0 hr (n = 61 cells) and 0.37 ± 0.02 at 7 hr (n = 65 cells; 3 seedlings each; p<0.0001; Mann–Whitney U test).
claims.source: Quantification of MT anisotropy showed a significant increase in MT anisotropy 7 hr after laceration (mean ± SE is 0.080 ± 0.007 for 0 hr, n = 61 cells and 0.37 ± 0.02 for 7 hr, n = 65 cells; 3 seedlings each; p<0.0001; Mann–Whitney U test), indicating that changes in tissue-wide stresses could override cellular level control of MT anisotropy.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of microtubule anisotropy with statistical significance testing.

claims.claim: Changes in tissue-wide stresses can override cellular level control of microtubule anisotropy.
claims.source: Quantification of MT anisotropy showed a significant increase in MT anisotropy 7 hr after laceration (mean ± SE is 0.080 ± 0.007 for 0 hr, n = 61 cells and 0.37 ± 0.02 for 7 hr, n = 65 cells; 3 seedlings each; p<0.0001; Mann–Whitney U test), indicating that changes in tissue-wide stresses could override cellular level control of MT anisotropy.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that tissue-level perturbations cause microtubule reorganization that is independent of cell shape.

claims.claim: After single-cell ablation, a circumferential rearrangement of stresses is observed, but less pronounced than after large-scale laceration, and observed only in cells adjacent to the site of perturbation.
claims.source: Similar to the large scale laceration experiments, a circumferential rearrangement of stresses was observed. However, the rearrangement was less pronounced than after cotyledon dissection, and observed in cells only adjacent to the site of perturbation (Figure 4A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results comparing single-cell and large-scale ablations.

claims.claim: Seven hours after single-cell ablation, microtubule alignment tends toward circumferential alignment around the ablated cell site, but is not completely circumferential.
claims.source: 7 hr after ablation, we observed that MT alignment had responded to treatment by tending toward a circumferential alignment around the ablated cell site. The MTs around the site of ablation were not completely circumferential, consistent with a scenario in which stress anisotropy is weaker in single cell ablation cases than in cases of large-scale dissection, therefore leading to a comparatively reduced alignment of MTs around the site of ablation (Figure 4C,D,E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental microtubule imaging data after single-cell ablation.

claims.claim: The microtubule alignment observed after single-cell ablation is significantly different from that resulting from large-scale perturbation.
claims.source: The alignment observed after single-cell ablation was significantly different from that resulting from large-scale perturbation, in which a strong circumferential response was obtained.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of microtubule responses to different scales of mechanical perturbation.

claims.claim: The majority of guard cells retain transverse microtubule arrays after large-scale ablation.
claims.source: Single optical sections show that MT arrays still remain transverse in majority of the guard cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) indicating that these cells retain a certain degree of control of their MTs while being under the influence of a directional force field.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental microtubule imaging data in guard cells after laceration.

claims.claim: Guard cells retain a certain degree of control of their microtubules while being under the influence of a directional force field.
claims.source: Single optical sections show that MT arrays still remain transverse in majority of the guard cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) indicating that these cells retain a certain degree of control of their MTs while being under the influence of a directional force field.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that guard cell microtubules maintain their transverse orientation despite tissue-level stress changes.

claims.claim: Treatment with 40 μM isoxaben for 16 hours leads to a sizeable increase in microtubule anisotropy, with mean ± SE of 0.27 ± 0.04 at 0 hr (n = 53 cells) and 0.54 ± 0.08 at 16 hr (n = 53 cells; 3 seedlings; p<0.0001, Mann–Whitney U test).
claims.source: Treatment of 3-day-old seedlings with 40 μM isoxaben for 16 hr led to a sizeable increase in the anisotropy of microtubules (mean ± SE is 0.27 ± 0.04 for 0 hr, n = 53 cells and 0.54 ± 0.08 for 16 hr, n = 53 cells; 3 seedlings; p<0.0001, Mann–Whitney U test; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of microtubule anisotropy after isoxaben treatment with statistical significance testing.

claims.claim: Isoxaben treatment induces hyperbundling and hyperalignment of cortical microtubules along predicted directions of maximal stress in shoot meristem cells.
claims.source: Isoxaben was shown previously to induce hyperbundling and hyperalignment of cortical microtubules along the predicted directions of maximal stress in shoot meristem cells (Heisler et al., 2010), consistent with increased stress levels in the cell walls compared to non-treated plants.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Heisler et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Homozygotes for the katanin loss-of-function allele ktn1-3 exhibit severe pavement cell shape defects.
claims.source: Homozygotes for the katanin loss-of-function allele ktn1-3 exhibit severe pavement cell shape defects, consistent with the role of MTs in neck formation (Lin et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Microtubule anisotropy in the bot 1-7 katanin allele shows a 60% reduction compared to wild type, with mean ± SE of 0.09 ± 0.01 for bot 1-7 (n = 83 cells; 4 seedlings) and 0.23 ± 0.05 for WT (n = 53 cells; 3 seedlings).
claims.source: When quantifying MT anisotropy in the bot 1-7 katanin allele, we found a 60% reduction when compared to the wild type (Mean ± SE is 0.09 ± 0.01 for bot 1-7, n = 83 cells; 4 seedling and 0.23 ± 0.05 for WT, n = 53 cells; 3 seedlings), thus confirming the relation between MT ordering and pavement cell shape.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements comparing microtubule anisotropy in mutant and wild-type plants.

claims.claim: In the shoot meristem, microtubule rearrangement after changes in mechanical stress is promoted by katanin-dependent microtubule severing.
claims.source: It has been shown in the shoot meristem that the response of MTs to tissue stress relies on MT self-organization. In particular, MT rearrangement after changes in mechanical stress is promoted by katanin-dependent MT severing (Uyttewaal et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Uyttewaal et al., 2012.

claims.claim: In bot1-7 mutants, microtubule arrays in pavement cells remain relatively isotropic after micromechanical perturbations (lacerations and compressions).
claims.source: In both assays, MT arrays in pavement cells remained relatively isotropic after the micromechanical perturbations (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–C; Video 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental microtubule imaging data in katanin mutant background after mechanical perturbations.

claims.claim: In bot 1-7 mutants, there is no significant difference in microtubule anisotropy before and 7 hours after ablation, with mean ± SE of 0.09 ± 0.02 at 0 hr (n = 83 cells) and 0.10 ± 0.02 at 7 hr (n = 74 cells; 3 seedlings; p>0.05, t test).
claims.source: Measurement of MT anisotropy showed no significant difference before and 7 hr after ablation in bot 1-7 (mean ± SE is 0.09 ± 0.02 for 0 hr, n = 83 cells and 0.10 ± 0.02 for 7 hr, n = 74 cells; 3 seedlings; p>0.05, t test; Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of microtubule anisotropy in katanin mutants with statistical testing.

claims.claim: The microtubule response to stress is conserved in different tissues and at different scales, and relies on a similar mechanism.
claims.source: These results are consistent with observations made in the shoot apical meristem (Uyttewaal et al., 2012) and suggest that the MT response to stress is not only conserved in different tissues and at different scales, but also relies on a similar mechanism.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of results in pavement cells with previously published results in shoot apical meristem.

claims.claim: Microtubule severing occurs at sites of crossover points of microtubules.
claims.source: Using time-series imaging of MT arrays, we could observe severing of MTs occurring at sites of crossover points of MTs (Figure 5A; Wightman and Turner, 2007; Lindeboom et al., 2013; Wightman et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data and is consistent with previously published observations.

claims.claim: The severing rate in mock-treated control seedlings is 0.08 ± 0.02 × 10−3 events μm−2 min−1 (mean ± SD, N = 16 cells, 4 seedlings, total area of 2.99 × 104 μm2).
claims.source: The severing rate in mock-treated control seedlings of 0.08 ± 0.02 × 10−3 events μm−2 min−1 (mean ± SD, N = 16 cells, 4 seedlings, total area of 2.99 × 104 μm2) is in agreement with what has been previously published (Wightman and Turner, 2007; Wightman et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of severing events and is consistent with previously published values.

claims.claim: In seedlings subjected to changes in mechanical forces, cell files close to the site of ablation show a significant increase in severing rate to 0.93 ± 0.45 × 10−3 events μm−2 min−1 (mean ± SD, N = 16 cells, 4 seedlings, total area of 1.5 × 104μm2, p<0.01, t test) 3 hours after ablation.
claims.source: However, in seedlings subjected to changes in mechanical forces, cell files close to the site of ablation showed a significant increase in severing rate to 0.93 ± 0.45 × 10−3 events μm−2 min−1 (mean ± SD, N = 16 cells, 4 seedlings, total area of 1.5 × 104μm2, p<0.01, t test) 3 hr after ablation (Figure 5B; Video 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of severing events after mechanical perturbation with statistical significance testing.

claims.claim: Cells experiencing changes in mechanical stress show a 65% decrease in the number of crossover points, with mean ± SE of 15 ± 3 per 10 μm2 at 0 hr (n = 6 cells) and 5 ± 2 per 10 μm2 at 3 hr.
claims.source: Measurement of number of crossover points (i.e., two polymerizing MT crossing each other without experiencing severing or catastrophe) immediately after and 3 hr after mock treatment showed a 9% increase (mean ± SE is 11.0 ± 1.4 per 10 μm2 for 0 hr, n = 6 cells and 12 ± 1.5 per 10 µm2 for 3 hr) whereas the cells experiencing changes in mechanical stress showed a 65% decrease in the number of cross over points (mean ± SE is 15 ± 3 per 10 μm2 for 0 hr, n = 6 cells and 5 ± 2 per 10 μm2 for 3 hr).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of microtubule crossover points before and after mechanical perturbation.

claims.claim: There is an up-regulation in the severing of microtubules at crossover sites after changes in mechanical stress.
claims.source: These measurements demonstrate an up-regulation in the severing of MTs at crossover sites after changes in mechanical stress.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined measurements of increased severing rate and decreased crossover points after mechanical perturbation.

claims.claim: Increased microtubule severing at crossover sites can enrich the population of free microtubules while removing microtubules that do not align parallel to maximal tensile stress, resulting in the generation of anisotropic microtubule arrays.
claims.source: This mechanism could enrich the population of free MTs, while removing the MTs that do not align parallel to maximal tensile stress, thereby resulting in the generation of anisotropic MT arrays.
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism inferred from the observed increase in severing and resulting microtubule alignment.

claims.claim: Pavement cell shape depends on mechanical heterogeneities.
claims.source: Here, we could correlate the behavior of the microtubular cytoskeleton with the predicted stress pattern and with quantified mechanical properties. This validates a number of previous studies assuming that pavement cell shape depends on mechanical heterogeneities (Fu et al., 2005), albeit relying only on MT behavior, and further supports plant tissues as facile systems to investigate the relation between the biophysics of growth and development.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the combined evidence from computational modeling, AFM measurements, and microtubule imaging, and validates previous assumptions.

claims.claim: Current models on pavement cell morphology suggest an influence of a ROP-based signaling mechanism on the cytoskeletal network.
claims.source: Current models on pavement cell morphology suggest an influence of a ROP-based signaling mechanism on the cytoskeletal network (Fu et al., 2005; Yang, 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fu et al., 2005 and Yang, 2008.

claims.claim: An auxin-dependent self-organizing mechanism controls the ROP-based signaling network.
claims.source: More recently it has been proposed that an auxin-dependent self-organizing mechanism controls the ROP-based signaling network (Xu et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Time lapse-imaging studies of pavement cell development show an initial phase of multiple lobe initiations, followed by a phase of isotropic expansion during which the cell shape is maintained.
claims.source: This model of differential growth is challenged by time lapse-imaging studies of pavement cell development, which shows an initial phase of multiple lobe initiations, followed by a phase of isotropic expansion during which the cell shape is maintained (Zhang et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Subcellular mechanical stresses control microtubule organization, which in turn affects the mechanical anisotropy of the cell wall thereby contributing to cell shape.
claims.source: In our study we show how subcellular mechanical stresses control MT organization, which in turn affects the mechanical anisotropy of the cell wall thereby contributing to cell shape irrespective of the previously proposed mechanisms.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined evidence of stress modeling, microtubule imaging, and AFM measurements.

claims.claim: Microtubule organization in the shoot meristem depends on tissue shape-derived stresses.
claims.source: Previous findings on the shoot meristem suggest that MT organization depends on tissue shape-derived stresses (Hamant et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hamant et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Cells can interpret mechanical signals that are generated by their own shape.
claims.source: Here, we found that cells can also interpret mechanical signals that are generated by their own shape.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that cell shape-derived stresses correlate with subcellular microtubule organization.

claims.claim: Microtubule behavior depends on stress intensity, which is cell autonomous as long as tissue stresses do not override it.
claims.source: As this response is lost in large-scale mechanical perturbations, we propose that MT behavior depends on stress intensity, which is cell autonomous as long as tissue stresses do not override it.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of microtubule responses to cell-scale versus tissue-scale mechanical perturbations.

claims.claim: Mechanical forces cause changes to single microtubule dynamics in vivo by regulating the activity of microtubule-associated proteins.
claims.source: Mechanical forces are known to cause changes to single MT dynamics in vivo by regulating the activity of MT-associated proteins (Trushko et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Trushko et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Tensile forces acting on the kinetochore complex-attached microtubule ends influence microtubule elongation rates during mitosis.
claims.source: In several organisms tensile forces acting on the kinetochore complex-attached MT ends are known to influence MT elongation rates during mitosis (Nicklas, 1988; Skibbens et al., 1993; Gardner et al., 2005; Franck et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nicklas, 1988; Skibbens et al., 1993; Gardner et al., 2005; Franck et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Katanin-mediated microtubule severing is required for microtubule response to changes in mechanical stresses in the shoot apical meristem.
claims.source: Previous studies on the shoot apical meristem show that katanin-mediated MT severing is required for MT response to changes in mechanical stresses (Uyttewaal et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Uyttewaal et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Severing itself is promoted by mechanical stress.
claims.source: Our data not only show that a similar mechanism is present in pavement cells, but also show that severing itself is promoted by mechanical stress.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the quantitative measurements showing increased severing rate after mechanical perturbation.

claims.claim: Conformation changes to the microtubule lattice act as hotspots promoting katanin binding and activity.
claims.source: Reports have shown that conformation changes to the MT lattice act as hotspots promoting katanin binding and activity (Davis et al., 2002; Díaz-Valencia et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Davis et al., 2002 and Díaz-Valencia et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Microtubule behavior depends on two parameters of mechanical stress: stress direction from cell and tissue shape determines the dominant microtubule orientation, and stress intensity modulates severing activity, which controls the response of microtubules to stress.
claims.source: MT behavior would thus depend on two parameters of mechanical stress (Figure 6): stress direction from cell and tissue shape determine the dominant MT orientation, which dictates wall reinforcement, and thus in turn contributes to cell and tissue shape; and stress intensity modulates severing activity, which controls the response of MTs to stress.
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model inferred from the combined experimental and computational results.

claims.claim: There is no need for several rules to explain microtubule behaviors at different scales or in different tissues in response to mechanical signals and perturbations.
claims.source: Based on these results, there is no need for several rules to explain MT behaviors at different scales or in different tissues in response to mechanical signals and perturbations, and this parsimony might be one of the defining features of mechanical signaling, when compared to molecular signaling.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that similar mechanisms operate at different scales and in different tissues.

claims.claim: The impact of mechanical forces on actin dynamics may have a similar multiscale role in animals as microtubules have in plants.
claims.source: As shape rather relies on the actomyosin network in animals, the impact of mechanical forces on actin dynamics may in principle have a similar multiscale role in animals.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential parallel mechanism in animal systems based on the findings in plants.

results.result: Microtubule arrays in indenting regions of pavement cells are significantly more anisotropic than in lobes (0.40 ± 0.02 vs 0.20 ± 0.02, p<0.01), and this anisotropy is maintained over time (0.47 ± 0.01 at 3 hours). This pattern is consistent on both inner and outer cell faces.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, and C9 provide converging quantitative evidence from nematic tensor analysis and time-lapse imaging showing differential microtubule organization in pavement cells. The statistical significance (p<0.01), adequate sample sizes (n=18 cells, 3 seedlings), and consistency with prior literature support this result.

results.result: AFM measurements reveal mechanical heterogeneities in pavement cell walls (2-8 MPa), with fibrous patterns of higher elastic modulus concentrated at indenting regions. These mechanical reinforcements correlate with microtubule organization and cellulose deposition, supporting a model where localized MT-dependent wall reinforcements maintain pavement cell shape.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C10 provide complementary evidence from AFM stiffness mapping, cellulose staining, and microtubule imaging. The AFM data directly demonstrate mechanical anisotropy matching predicted cellulose microfibril patterns, validating the mechanical basis of the shape maintenance model. The guard cell validation (C3, C4) establishes the reliability of the AFM approach.

results.result: 3D finite element modeling predicts that cell geometry generates anisotropic stress patterns focused in indenting regions, and these predicted stress directions correlate well with observed microtubule arrangements. The stress pattern is determined primarily by cell geometry rather than material anisotropy for small elastic deformations.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C18 present computational modeling results that are validated against experimental observations. The correlation between predicted stress patterns and observed microtubule organization is demonstrated across multiple model geometries. However, the model relies on several assumptions (turgor pressure, material properties, boundary conditions) that are acknowledged but not fully validated experimentally.

results.result: Microtubule organization responds to tissue topography: elevated stomata show circumferential microtubule patterns consistent with predicted stress directions, while non-elevated stomata do not. This correlation between mechanical stress and microtubule orientation extends from supracellular to subcellular scales.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C23 provide experimental validation of model predictions using stomata as a natural test case. The presence of circumferential patterns only around elevated stomata (C20, C21) supports the mechanical stress hypothesis. The inference that this mechanism operates at multiple scales (C22, C23) is reasonable given the combined evidence.

results.result: Mechanical compression of cotyledon pavement cells results in cell flattening and a significant, reversible increase in microtubule anisotropy (from 0.37 ± 0.06 to 0.57 ± 0.06 at 7 hours, p<0.0001). Upon release of compression, microtubule anisotropy returns to near-baseline levels (0.24 ± 0.02 at 24 hours).
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C28 demonstrate a causal relationship between mechanical stress and microtubule organization through experimental manipulation. The quantitative measurements with appropriate statistical testing (Mann-Whitney U test, p<0.0001) and adequate sample sizes (n=95 cells, 5 seedlings) support the result. The authors acknowledge that imaging conditions differ between timepoints, which could affect absolute values, but the trend is clear.

results.result: Large-scale tissue laceration causes immediate tissue deformation consistent with tension release and induces progressive circumferential microtubule alignment around the wound site. Microtubule anisotropy increases significantly (from 0.080 ± 0.007 to 0.37 ± 0.02 at 7 hours, p<0.0001), demonstrating that tissue-wide stresses can override cellular-level control of microtubule organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34 provide strong evidence through combined modeling, tissue deformation analysis, and time-lapse imaging. The progressive nature of the response (3.5 to 7 hours) and independence from cell shape support the interpretation that tissue-level stresses dominate. Statistical significance is well-established (p<0.0001). However, the authors acknowledge that wound responses could involve both mechanical and biochemical signals.

results.result: Single-cell ablation produces weaker, more localized stress rearrangements and correspondingly weaker microtubule responses compared to large-scale perturbations. Microtubules show partial circumferential alignment around ablated cells but not complete reorganization, indicating that microtubule response depends on stress magnitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 demonstrate scale-dependent responses through comparison of single-cell versus tissue-level perturbations. Both computational modeling and experimental observations support the conclusion that stress intensity affects microtubule response magnitude. This provides important evidence for the hierarchical nature of mechanical control.

results.result: Guard cells retain transverse microtubule arrays even after large-scale tissue ablation, indicating cell-type-specific control of microtubule organization that can resist tissue-level mechanical signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C38 and C39 provide evidence for cell-autonomous control mechanisms that can override tissue-level mechanical signals. The observation is clearly documented through imaging, though the mechanism underlying this resistance is not explored. This represents an important exception to the general stress-response model.

results.result: Treatment with the cellulose synthase inhibitor isoxaben (40 μM for 16 hours) causes a significant increase in microtubule anisotropy (from 0.27 ± 0.04 to 0.54 ± 0.08, p<0.0001), consistent with increased mechanical stress in cell walls.
results.evaluation: Claims C40 and C41 provide pharmacological evidence supporting the mechanical stress hypothesis. The significant increase in microtubule anisotropy with appropriate statistical testing supports the interpretation. The connection to prior work in shoot meristem (C41) strengthens the conclusion, though the authors acknowledge that more complex scenarios involving both mechanics and other responses cannot be ruled out.

results.result: The katanin mutant bot1-7 shows 60% reduced microtubule anisotropy compared to wild-type and fails to reorganize microtubules in response to mechanical perturbations (compression and laceration). This demonstrates that katanin-dependent microtubule severing is required for stress-responsive microtubule reorganization in pavement cells, similar to the shoot meristem.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C47 provide strong genetic evidence for the mechanism of microtubule response to stress. The quantitative comparison between wild-type and mutant (C43), lack of response to perturbations (C45, C46), and consistency with prior work in different tissues (C44, C47) all support the conclusion. Sample sizes are adequate and statistical testing appropriate (p>0.05 for no difference in mutant).

results.result: Mechanical stress increases microtubule severing rate at crossover sites from 0.08 ± 0.02 × 10⁻³ to 0.93 ± 0.45 × 10⁻³ events μm⁻² min⁻¹ (p<0.01) within 3 hours of ablation. This is accompanied by a 65% decrease in crossover points, demonstrating stress-dependent upregulation of severing activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 provide direct quantitative evidence for the mechanism linking stress to microtubule reorganization. The baseline severing rate (C49) is consistent with published values, and the significant increase after perturbation (C50) with appropriate statistical testing supports the conclusion. The complementary measurement of crossover point reduction (C51) strengthens the interpretation of increased severing activity.

results.result: Increased microtubule severing at crossover sites is proposed to enrich free microtubules while removing those not aligned with maximal tensile stress, generating anisotropic microtubule arrays.
results.evaluation: Claim C53 presents a mechanistic model that is plausible given the observed increase in severing and resulting alignment, but it remains speculative. The authors appropriately use conditional language ('could enrich'). Direct evidence for the proposed enrichment mechanism (e.g., tracking individual microtubule dynamics, measuring free microtubule populations) is not provided.

results.result: Subcellular mechanical stresses derived from cell shape control microtubule organization, which affects cell wall mechanical anisotropy and contributes to cell shape maintenance. Cells can interpret mechanical signals from their own shape, and this cell-autonomous response persists unless overridden by stronger tissue-level stresses.
results.evaluation: Claims C54, C58, C60, and C61 synthesize the major findings into a coherent model. The integration of AFM data, computational modeling, and perturbation experiments provides strong support. The hierarchical nature of mechanical control (cell vs. tissue level) is well-demonstrated through the scale-dependent perturbation experiments. This represents the central conceptual advance of the paper.

results.result: Microtubule behavior depends on two parameters of mechanical stress: stress direction (from cell and tissue shape) determines dominant microtubule orientation, and stress intensity modulates severing activity. This unified mechanism operates across scales and tissues without requiring multiple distinct rules.
results.evaluation: Claims C67 and C68 present an integrative model supported by the combined experimental and computational results. The parsimony of the model (single mechanism across scales) is supported by the consistency of observations in pavement cells with prior work in shoot meristem. However, C67 includes speculative elements about the precise relationship between stress and katanin activity that are not fully validated.

results.result: Prior models of pavement cell morphology invoke ROP-based signaling, auxin-dependent self-organization, and differential growth mechanisms, but time-lapse studies challenge the differential growth model by showing isotropic expansion after initial lobe formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 accurately summarize prior work through appropriate citations. These claims provide context for the current study but do not present new findings. The accuracy of these summaries depends on the cited literature.

results.result: Previous work in shoot meristem demonstrates that microtubule organization depends on tissue shape-derived stresses.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 accurately cites prior work (Hamant et al., 2008) that established the stress-microtubule relationship in a different tissue context. This provides important precedent for the current study.

results.result: Prior work demonstrates that mechanical forces affect microtubule dynamics through regulation of microtubule-associated proteins, including effects on elongation rates during mitosis and katanin-mediated severing in shoot meristem. Conformational changes to the microtubule lattice promote katanin binding and activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C62, C63, C64, and C66 accurately cite relevant prior work establishing precedents for mechanosensitive microtubule regulation. These provide important context and mechanistic hypotheses for the current findings.

results.result: Severing activity itself is promoted by mechanical stress in pavement cells, extending beyond previous findings that severing is required for stress response.
results.evaluation: Claim C65 represents a novel finding supported by the quantitative severing measurements (C50). This advances understanding beyond prior work showing that katanin is required for stress response, by demonstrating that stress actively promotes severing activity.

results.result: The impact of mechanical forces on actin dynamics may have a similar multiscale role in animals as microtubules have in plants.
results.evaluation: Claim C69 is explicitly speculative ('may in principle'), proposing a potential parallel in animal systems. No evidence is provided to support this speculation, and the authors appropriately present it as a hypothesis rather than a conclusion.
